title: Brass bands, high and low class music and Jim Crow
summary: Steinau saw only Mardi Gras marching bands; they discuss class and racial divisions in the music of his youth and the lack of white brass bands.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Well, it, uh, no, I just don't think of that as being a particular parade neighborhood.

Well, it wasn't and I don't think, I don't think. I don't know that I ever saw a marching band except in Mardi Gras parades. Mm-hmm. Which of course I saw a lot of, but I'm not sure how much I listened to them. I don't think I did. Uh.
No, it wasn't anything anybody would comment on, I guess, except on a, or casual panel. It's something everybody took for granted, is my impression.

Well, also, you know, there was, there was not necessarily only the Jim Crow business when I was a kid and coming up, but there was also the business that there was high class and low class type music as far as, as well as a number of other. Mm-hmm. You know, I, I think this sort of applied to a lot of other things.
Yeah, well, I mean, you wouldn't run over to Magazine Street and hear, say, a white brass band. No.

Playing a white jazz brass band, which most people don't even know exist hardly. Yeah. I don't think we'll, but we didn't go take pictures of things. I still hear them once in a while. Did. Oh, brass bands? White brass bands.
